headings.title: Introduction to Comprehensive Patient Assessment
headings.content: Comprehensive patient assessment is the foundational first step of the nursing process, serving as the cornerstone of safe, individualized nursing care in medical-surgical settings. It involves the systematic and continuous collection, validation, organization, and communication of patient data. For nursing students in Nigeria, mastering assessment means understanding both subjective data—what the patient tells you during the interview, such as pain or nausea—and objective data—what you observe, measure, or discover through physical examination and diagnostic tests, such as vital signs or surgical incision status. A thorough assessment enables the nurse to establish a baseline, identify actual or potential health problems, formulate accurate nursing diagnoses, and evaluate the effectiveness of nursing interventions over time. Holistic assessment goes beyond mere physiological measurements; it encompasses the physical, psychological, sociocultural, and spiritual dimensions of the patient. Cultivating strong clinical judgment during the assessment phase allows nurses to detect subtle signs of clinical deterioration early, thereby preventing adverse events and improving patient outcomes in diverse healthcare environments across Nigeria. Systematic data collection also fosters therapeutic nurse-patient relationships, encouraging patients to actively participate in their own care plans and promoting health literacy from admission to discharge.

headings.title: Health History and Biographical Data Collection
headings.content: The health history and biographical data collection form the narrative backbone of a comprehensive nursing assessment. Biographical data includes demographic information such as age, gender, occupation, primary language, and support systems, which provide essential context regarding the patient's socioeconomic background and potential access to healthcare resources in Nigeria. The health history begins with the chief complaint or reason for seeking care, captured in the patient's own words. Following this, the nurse systematically explores the history of the present illness (HPI) using analytical attributes such as location, quality, severity, timing, and aggravating or relieving factors. Past medical and surgical history, family health history, allergies, current medications, and a comprehensive review of systems (ROS) are then documented. Conducting a successful health history interview requires effective communication skills, including active listening, open-ended questioning, empathy, and cultural sensitivity. For Nigerian nursing students, it is vital to be mindful of local cultural nuances, language barriers, and traditional beliefs that may influence how patients perceive and report their symptoms. Accurate collection of biographical and historical data prevents diagnostic errors, respects patient autonomy, and ensures that care plans are tailored specifically to the individual's unique lifestyle and health needs.

headings.title: Techniques of Physical Examination: Inspection, Palpation, Percussion, and Auscultation
headings.content: Physical examination relies on four foundational techniques: inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation. Mastery of these skills is essential for detecting clinical abnormalities. Inspection is the deliberate, focused observation of the patient's body, noting symmetry, color, size, shape, and abnormal movements, beginning the moment the nurse meets the patient. Palpation involves using the sense of touch to evaluate texture, temperature, moisture, swelling, tenderness, pulsations, and masses. Different parts of the hand are used for specific sensations, such as the palmar surface for masses and the dorsal surface for temperature. Percussion utilizes striking the body surface with short, sharp taps to produce sound waves that help determine the density, size, and borders of underlying organs, yielding tones such as tympany, resonance, or dullness. Auscultation is listening to sounds produced within the body—such as heart sounds, breath sounds, bowel sounds, and vascular bruits—using a stethoscope. Unlike the standard sequence for other body systems, abdominal assessment requires auscultation to be performed before palpation and percussion to avoid altering natural bowel motility and producing false findings. Practicing these techniques methodically ensures accurate physical data collection, which is critical for formulating sound nursing diagnoses and collaborating effectively with the interprofessional healthcare team in Nigerian hospitals.

headings.title: System-by-System Physical Assessment
headings.content: System-by-system physical assessment provides a structured, logical framework for evaluating every major organ system in the human body, ensuring no area is overlooked during a comprehensive medical-surgical examination. This structured approach typically moves from general survey and neurological status to cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, musculoskeletal, and integumentary systems. For example, a cardiovascular assessment includes evaluating blood pressure, peripheral pulses, capillary refill, heart sounds (S1 and S2), and checking for dependent edema. Respiratory assessment focuses on rate, rhythm, depth of breathing, symmetry of chest expansion, use of accessory muscles, and auscultating for adventitious breath sounds like crackles, wheezes, or pleural friction rubs. Musculoskeletal evaluation examines range of motion, muscle strength grading, joint stability, and symmetry. Throughout each system assessment, nurses must integrate critical thinking to connect physical findings with underlying pathophysiology. For instance, diminished breath sounds combined with dullness to percussion over the lung bases may indicate a pleural effusion requiring immediate medical attention. By systematically moving from head to toe or system by system, nursing students develop clinical competence and confidence, ensuring that abnormal findings are promptly identified, documented, and reported to the attending physician or healthcare team in clinical practice.

headings.title: Pain Assessment and Management Strategies
headings.content: Pain is widely recognized as the fifth vital sign and represents a complex, subjective experience influenced by physiological, psychological, and sociocultural factors. Effective pain assessment requires the nurse to utilize validated pain rating scales appropriate for the patient's developmental age and cognitive status, such as the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), Verbal Descriptor Scale, or Wong-Baker FACES scale for pediatric or cognitively impaired patients. A comprehensive pain assessment follows the PQRST mnemonic: P for Provocative/Palliative factors, Q for Quality, R for Region/Radiation, S for Severity, and T for Timing. Nurses must remember that pain is whatever the experiencing person says it is and exists whenever the person says it does, making patient self-report the gold standard. Management strategies combine pharmacological interventions—such as non-opioid analgesics, adjuvants, and opioids based on the WHO analgesic ladder—with non-pharmacological modalities like repositioning, heat and cold therapy, distraction, massage, and relaxation techniques. In Nigerian healthcare settings, cultural beliefs regarding pain expression can vary significantly; some patients may stoically endure severe pain, while others may express it overtly. Nurses must provide individualized, compassionate care, continuously re-assessing pain levels following interventions to ensure patient comfort, prevent chronic pain development, and promote recovery.

headings.title: Psychosocial, Cultural, and Spiritual Assessment
headings.content: Holistic nursing care demands a thorough evaluation of the psychosocial, cultural, and spiritual dimensions of every patient. Psychosocial assessment explores the patient's mental status, emotional state, coping mechanisms, self-concept, occupational stress, and family or social support networks. Mental health conditions, anxiety, and depression frequently coexist with physical illnesses in medical-surgical wards and can significantly impact recovery rates. Cultural assessment examines the patient's ethnic background, values, health beliefs, language preferences, dietary practices, and traditional healing methods. In multicultural nations like Nigeria, recognizing and respecting diverse cultural frameworks—such as beliefs surrounding illness causation, birth, and death—is essential for building trust and ensuring adherence to care plans. Spiritual assessment investigates the patient's source of meaning, hope, faith, and religious practices that may provide comfort during severe illness or end-of-life care. Nurses must remain non-judgmental, practicing cultural humility and actively collaborating with pastoral care workers or family elders when appropriate. By integrating psychosocial, cultural, and spiritual data into the nursing care plan, nurses honor the dignity of the whole person, reduce healthcare disparities, and foster an environment conducive to optimal physical and emotional healing.

headings.title: Interpreting Diagnostic and Laboratory Findings
headings.content: Interpreting diagnostic and laboratory findings is an essential competency for modern medical-surgical nurses, bridging the gap between subjective-objective clinical data and underlying pathophysiology. Laboratory tests encompass hematology (such as complete blood count for detecting anemia or infection), clinical chemistry (such as electrolytes, renal function tests like creatinine and BUN, and liver enzymes), coagulation profiles, and urinalysis. Diagnostic imaging and studies include chest radiographs, computed tomography (CT) scans, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and electrocardiograms (ECGs). Nurses must understand normal reference ranges, recognize critical panic values that require immediate medical intervention, and correlate lab results with the patient's clinical presentation. For example, an elevated white blood cell count (leukocytosis) alongside fever and localized abdominal tenderness strongly suggests an inflammatory or infectious process such as acute appendicitis. Furthermore, nurses play a key role in patient preparation, safe specimen collection, monitoring for post-procedure complications, and educating patients on what to expect. Accurate interpretation empowers nurses to participate actively in multidisciplinary clinical rounds, advocate for timely medical treatments, and monitor the progression or resolution of disease states effectively in Nigerian healthcare institutions.

headings.title: Documentation and Reporting in Medical-Surgical Nursing
headings.content: Documentation and reporting are critical legal, professional, and clinical responsibilities in medical-surgical nursing. Accurate documentation creates a permanent legal record of the nursing care provided, tracks patient progress, facilitates communication among the interprofessional healthcare team, and supports quality improvement and reimbursement processes. Nursing documentation must adhere to professional standards: it must be accurate, objective, legible, timely, and concise, avoiding vague terms like 'good' or 'normal'. Commonly used charting formats include SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan), PIE (Problem, Intervention, Evaluation), and narrative charting, as well as electronic health records (EHRs). Alongside written documentation, verbal reporting—such as structured handovers using the SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) tool—ensures seamless transitions of care during shift changes or patient transfers between departments. In Nigerian nursing practice, maintaining patient confidentiality and data privacy, in accordance with professional codes of ethics and legal statutes, is paramount. Every entry must include the date, time, and the nurse's signature with professional designation. Failure to document accurately can compromise patient safety and leaves the nurse legally vulnerable; therefore, the golden rule remains: if it was not charted, legally, it was not done.
